column3: It repeats the decree-to-Kun-to-occurrence sequence and frames it as unmediated creation.
It states the performative command most directly: divine speech brings the intended thing into being.
A report of what people used to say adds no clear link to life, death, decree, or effective command.
The same formula grounds creation without offspring, adding a polemical application of the focus's command.
The immediately preceding staged human life supplies the embodied process that 40:68 attributes to God's power over life and death.
Its instruction for upright speech in care of heirs does not illuminate the divine command in the focus.
It closely restates will, address, Kun, and occurrence as one sovereign act.
The gift of guidance and scripture to Moses belongs to the surah's message-to-command progression but is not specific to the focus.
A matter already decreed before its visible unfolding clarifies how a settled command opens into events in time.
The repeated Kun formula applies the focus's creative command to Mary's question about birth.
Creation of heavens and earth establishes the greater creative capacity behind reviving human beings.
Its irrevocably settled decree concerns approach to Hell rather than the focus's life-giving command.
It directly joins God's giving life and death to a call for reflection.
A divine decision removes a human alternative, clarifying one consequence of a settled command without equating human and creative decree.
A disputed claim about faith does not develop divine life, death, decree, or command.
It directly names God as the giver of life and death and adds return to Him.
Protection from evils and mercy provide nearby judgment context but not the focus's command sequence.
The contrast between claiming to hear and truly hearing is not a clear counterpart to the creative utterance.
Creation from clay and fixed terms place human life within a measured and appointed determination.
The creatures' fear and obedience depict an enacted response to command, though not creative command itself.
The retrospective question about punishment adds no specific account of command becoming event.
It explicitly connects true creation, Kun, occurrence, and the Day when sovereignty is manifest.
The same surah's call to invoke God sincerely supplies the devotional response to the sovereign Lord of the focus.
Moses's self-identification as messenger is too general to clarify the focus.
Exclusive lordship is immediately expressed through power to give life and death.
The command to announce warning reflects authoritative speech but not its creative execution.
The admission of not being among those who pray gives only an indirect contrast to obedience before God.
The dispute tests the unique claim to give life and death, exposing its difference from human pretension.
Within the surah, opposed calls distinguish summons to disbelief from a call to the Mighty Forgiver.
The promised Hell made present illustrates a warning fulfilled, but not the focus's life-and-command relation.
It combines exclusive deity, life and death, and the summons to believe and follow God's words.
A plea for plague removal shows a conditional appeal under affliction, not the unresisted creative command.
The loss of human supporters does not add to the focus's account of divine decree.
A single cry followed by immediate sight supplies a compact resurrection analogue to command becoming event.
Same-surah dispute over God's signs gives broad resistance context without clarifying the focus's mechanism.
The repeated denial of resurrection is a useful contrary posture to the life-giving power affirmed in the focus.
Human creation from a drop supports the surah's creative setting but not its decree-and-Kun sequence.
Jesus's receipt of scripture and prophethood belongs to the surrounding decree narrative but adds little by itself.
Its instruction for kind speech in financial guardianship is unrelated to the focus.
The arrival of a messenger followed by a just decision shows command and judgment reaching a determinate outcome.
The futile call of disbelievers after warning is nearby judgment context rather than creative command.
The question of who owns earth prepares recognition of divine sovereignty but does not state life, death, or decree.
The terse reference to distributors of command suggests ordered execution but offers no further connection.
Death occurs only by God's permission at a written term, specifying the appointed limit behind divine control of life and death.
The warning against attributing offspring does not itself clarify the focus's command.
One cry as the decisive trigger for the eschatological event parallels immediate execution.
Moses's sending with signs and authority contributes only general same-surah message context.
Boasting over wealth and followers does not illuminate the focus.
When God's command arrives, judgment is settled in truth and falsehood loses, extending decree into final adjudication.
Kindness to one's mother and avoidance of tyranny do not add to the focus.
A false profession of belief does not bear on divine life, death, or effective command.
The immediate appearance after the cry completes the resurrection sequence begun by the preceding candidate.
Belief after seeing punishment failing to benefit gives same-surah finality context but not the focus's mechanism.
The reminder of creation from dust and drop reinforces the staged human origin immediately preceding the focus.
Adam's creation is explicitly explained through the Kun-and-occurrence formula.
The matter being decided on the Day of Regret supplies an eschatological instance of irreversible decree.
Lot's offer does not illuminate the focus's themes.
Universal dominion is expressed directly through God's giving life and death.
Past nations seized for sin provide nearby surah judgment context without a specific decree-to-event link.
The traveler's request for food is unrelated to the focus.
It lays out life, death, and renewed life in direct sequence, while exposing human ingratitude.
Ritual completion and vows do not clarify the focus's creative command.
Moses's objection to the damaged ship is unrelated to the focus.
Warning the living and the word becoming due against disbelievers gives a limited judgment-side parallel.
Rejection of clear messengers followed by punishment gives same-surah consequence context only.
Shu'ayb's call to reverence is too general to add to the focus.
God's ownership is paired with giving life and death and the absence of any protector besides Him.
God takes souls in death and sleep, retaining or releasing them to a fixed term, specifying one mode of His life-and-death rule.
Moses's request not to be blamed for forgetfulness is unrelated to the focus.
Abraham's confession that God will cause his death and then revive him gives a personal life-death formulation.
Provision through night and day has no specific bearing on decree, life, death, or Kun.
A plea for help against corrupters does not clarify the focus's sovereign command.
It concisely attributes both death and life to God alone.
Divine aid to messengers and believers is same-surah promise context but not a direct parallel.
Exclusive worship without association supports divine uniqueness but not the focus's life-death command.
The question joins God as life-giver and death-giver to His governance of every affair.
Mary's withdrawal begins the narrative but does not itself illuminate the focus.
A merciful Lord's utterance of peace shows authoritative speech with an outcome, though not creation or resurrection.
Post-pilgrimage remembrance and a worldly prayer do not clarify the focus.
The command to proclaim openly illustrates commissioned speech, not the focus's unresisted creative speech.
Confession that God is Lord and protection of worship spaces gives a broad monotheistic setting only.
Human failure to fulfill what was commanded contrasts with the focus's command that is never impeded in becoming real.
Prayer and almsgiving in Jesus's charge do not add to the focus's creative mechanism.
Jonah's prior glorification does not clarify life, death, decree, or Kun in this isolated verse.
It gives the full arc from death to life, death, renewed life, and return to God.
Turning away from God's signs supplies a general contrary response, not a link to the focus's command.
The accusation against Moses gives no specific contribution to the focus.
It corrects fatalistic regret by affirming that God gives life and death, though the military setting is distinct.
The command to inspect the fate of deniers offers broad warning context only.
The declaration of a previously disputed reality does not specify life, death, or divine command.
God's creating and guiding role begins a larger confession but this verse alone does not reach life, death, or Kun.
A request for delay does not clarify the focus.
The description of speech as decisive supports authoritative discourse but not its creative realization.
The messenger's complaint to his Lord records disbelief but adds no particular connection to the focus.
Rules for completing pilgrimage do not illuminate the focus's themes.
Repentance at death arriving too late supplies a boundary of finality around the focus's death motif.
A destructive assumption about God is too general to clarify the focus.
Gentle speech when unable to give material help is unrelated to the focus.
God's command suddenly reducing worldly growth to harvest shows an enacted command, but not life or Kun specifically.
Acknowledging God as creator without following its implications supplies a limited contrast to recognizing His sovereign power.
God commands striking the slain man, then explicitly says He gives life to the dead and shows His signs.
The man made to die and revived after a hundred years gives a concrete demonstration of resurrection by divine power.
The revivified birds directly demonstrate God's power to restore life after dispersal.
Bringing living from dead and dead from living articulates God's reversal of apparently fixed states.
Jesus's reviving of the dead by God's permission distinguishes divine life-giving from a messenger's delegated sign.
God's raising of the dead supplies a direct resurrection counterpart to the focus's life-giving authority.
Daily taking in sleep and reviving to an appointed term clarifies a recurring mode of divine control over life.
God brings living from dead and dead from living, directly developing the transformation implied by life and death.
Life, death, and later emergence from the earth are explicitly assigned to God's decree.
The challenge asks who originates creation and then restores it, pairing first creation with return.
Rain reviving dead earth gives a visible analogue for divine restoration to life.
God creates, causes death, and may return a person to feebleness, extending His authority across the lifespan.
The objection to being raised from bones and dust states the resurrection question answered by the focus's creative command.
The denial of restoration after becoming bones is answered by reference to the One who first created them.
Life, death, and being raised are marked as decisive divinely governed thresholds.
Jesus's speech joins birth, death, and resurrection in one life-course under God.
Humanity's origin from earth, return to it, and later extraction concisely frames resurrection.
Making every living thing from water establishes a universal creation basis for the focus's life-giving claim.
Every soul tasting death gives the universal limit over which the focus asserts divine control.
Staged human formation, death, and revival of dead earth explicitly argue for resurrection.
It declares that God gives life to the dead and has power over all things.
It explicitly affirms the coming Hour and God's resurrection of those in graves.
The certainty of death supplies the first half of the death-and-restoration sequence.
Resurrection on the Day of Rising completes the sequence immediately following death.
It directly states bringing living from dead, dead from living, and reviving the earth as the pattern for emergence.
Creation, provision, death, and renewed life are gathered as exclusive divine acts.
The reviving of earth after its death is explicitly offered as evidence of resurrection.
The angel of death taking souls and the return to God specify the death-side of the focus's authority.
God sends wind, revives dead land, and explicitly compares this to resurrection.
Giving life to the dead and recording what they sent ahead connects resurrection with an effective divine determination.
Dead land revived to yield food gives a material sign of the life-giving power stated in the focus.
The single trumpet blast followed by emergence from graves is a direct eschatological execution scene.
Creation from a drop confronts the human who disputes the possibility of restoration.
The question of who revives decayed bones directly poses the issue answered by the focus.
The answer assigns revival to the One who originated creation the first time.
The objection to being raised after becoming dust and bones forms a direct resurrection contrast.
Creation in stages within wombs and successive formations supplies a close creation-process parallel.
The confession of two deaths and two lives is the closest same-surah expansion of the focus's life-and-death authority.
Reviving dead earth is explicitly said to prove that its giver of life will revive the dead.
God's giving life to dead earth is tied to His power over all things.
Rain enlivening a dead land is followed by the explicit comparison to human emergence.
God gives life, causes death, then gathers all at the Day without doubt.
The Creator of heavens and earth is declared able to give life to the dead.
God alone gives life and death, and to Him is the final destination.
The fixed apportionment of death makes mortality part of an unthwarted divine determination.
Knowledge of the first creation is presented as grounds for recognizing re-creation.
Creating death and life explicitly attributes both poles to God as purposeful acts.
The denial that scattered bones will be gathered states the resurrection issue in its most compressed form.
The One who creates from a drop is explicitly affirmed able to give life to the dead.
Human ingratitude is set against the Creator's prior act of bringing the person into being.
Resurrection after death is stated as an act God performs whenever He wills.
The command to consider one's origin directs attention to the created basis of later restoration.
The Creator of the human from a gushing fluid is explicitly able to return him.
